title: Physicists Can't Agree on How the Universe Works
summary: Imagine asking 1,000 scientists a simple question: how does the universe work? Turns out, they can't agree! A new survey — the largest ever of physicists — found that experts disagree on almost everything. They argued about dark matter (mysterious stuff we can't see), black holes, and how to combine gravity with quantum mechanics (the rules for tiny particles). Even the standard model of cosmology, which is like the basic rulebook for the universe, didn't get majority support. Only two questions got a clear majority. One was about the Big Bang. Most people think the Big Bang was the beginning of time. But 68% of physicists said no — it just describes how the universe grew from a super hot, dense state. It doesn't explain whether time actually started then. Dark matter was another big disagreement. Only 17% thought it's made of undiscovered tiny particles. Another 12% said maybe we need to change our theory of gravity. The biggest group — 21% — said it's probably a mix of ideas. So is all this disagreement bad? Not at all, says scientist Niayesh Afshordi. He thinks it shows where the exciting discoveries might happen next. "There is a crack in everything, that's how the light gets in," he said, quoting a famous song. In science, not knowing is often the first step to finding out.
why_it_matters: It shows that even the smartest experts don't know everything, and that asking questions and admitting you're unsure is exactly how science moves forward.

background_read: Cosmology is the study of the whole universe — how it began and how it works.
The Big Bang is the leading idea about how the universe started, and astronomers have found evidence for it, such as the faint leftover heat from the very early universe.
Quantum mechanics (the rules for tiny particles) and gravity (the force that pulls things together) are two big ideas that physicists still cannot fit together in one theory.
Article_Structure: WHO: Physicists around the world who answered the biggest survey ever done, plus scientist Niayesh Afshordi.
WHAT: A survey showing that experts disagree about dark matter, black holes, gravity and quantum mechanics, and even the standard model of cosmology.
WHERE: A worldwide survey, with answers collected from physicists in many different countries.
WHY: To find out where physicists agree and where they don't — and to spot where new discoveries might happen next.

perspectives.description: They think disagreement is a good sign, because it shows where the next big discoveries might be hiding.
Some may feel that after many years of work, not agreeing on the basics makes it hard to know what to study next.
They may be surprised that the experts who study the universe don't agree on what most of it is even made of.
